references.text: The rich man's steward was cast out – here it is Lazarus who is "cast" (ἐβέβλητο) at the gate, an image of his helpless state ([ref:Luk 16:3|Luke 16:3]).
The rich man lived in extravagant luxury – Lazarus' poverty and sickness in verse 20 stand in sharp contrast to this ([ref:Luk 16:19|Luke 16:19]).
The continuation describes how Lazarus longed for the crumbs from the rich man's table, and dogs came and licked his sores ([ref:Luk 16:21|Luke 16:21]).
Job was struck with painful boils from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head, which recalls Lazarus' condition with sores all over his body ([ref:Job 2:7|Job 2:7]).
Isaiah describes wounds, bruises, and open wounds that are not bandaged – an image of physical suffering resembling Lazarus' sores ([ref:Jes 1:6|Isaiah 1:6]).
"The poor is hated even by his neighbor" – the proverb illustrates the situation of the poor Lazarus at the rich man's gate ([ref:Ordsp 14:20|Proverbs 14:20]).
"All the poor man's brothers hate him; how much more do his friends keep away" – Lazarus' isolation and misery reflect this ([ref:Ordsp 19:7|Proverbs 19:7]).
Lazarus in Bethany, brother of Mary and Martha, shares a name with the poor Lazarus in the parable. Both names mean "God helps" ([ref:Joh 11:1|John 11:1]).
The lame man was placed at the temple gate to beg – similarly, Lazarus was laid at the rich man's gate ([ref:Apg 3:2|Acts 3:2]).
God has chosen those who are poor in the world's eyes to be rich in faith and heirs of the kingdom – Lazarus is an example of this principle ([ref:Jak 2:5|James 2:5]).

"Blessed are you who are poor, for yours is the kingdom of God ... Blessed are you who weep now, for you shall laugh" – Lazarus' earthly suffering and heavenly comfort illustrate these beatitudes ([ref:Luk 6:20-21|Luke 6:20-21]).
